title: The Mughal Empire
description: An illustrated map of the Mughal Empire, from Babur’s boyhood in Ferghana and the battle of Panipat in 1526, through Akbar, the Taj Mahal and Aurangzeb’s wars with the Marathas, to the exile of the last emperor in 1858.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of the Mughal Empire from 1494 to 1862
note: Based on the Mughals’ own memoirs and court histories (the Baburnama, the Akbarnama, the Jahangirnama), European travellers, Sikh, Maratha and Rajput sources and modern historians; each chapter says which it follows. Army sizes and death tolls from chronicles are given as they state them and are disputed. The map is stylised and not to scale; Fatehpur Sikri is moved a little west so its pin does not sit on Agra’s. The Powers areas are painted loosely: borders shifted constantly.

steps.title: A prince of Ferghana
steps.text: Babur is born in 1483 in the Ferghana valley, descended from the conqueror Timur on his father’s side and from Chinggis Khan on his mother’s. In 1494, aged eleven, he inherits his father’s small kingdom, with its capital at Andijan. His memoir, the Baburnama, written in Chagatai Turkic, tells his story with rare frankness.
steps.today: Today: Andijan, in the Ferghana valley, Uzbekistan.

steps.title: Samarkand won and lost
steps.text: Babur dreams of Timur’s old capital, Samarkand. He takes it in 1497 but holds it only about a hundred days, and loses Andijan while he is away. He wins Samarkand again in 1500; then in 1501 Muhammad Shaybani Khan’s Uzbeks defeat him and drive him out. For three years he wanders, a king without a kingdom.
steps.today: Today: Samarkand, Uzbekistan.

steps.title: A kingdom in Kabul
steps.text: In 1504 Babur crosses the Hindu Kush and takes Kabul, which becomes his home. In 1507 he takes the title emperor (padishah). A last attempt on Samarkand, with help from Safavid Persia, fails in 1512. He lays out gardens, and from 1519 raids across the Indus into the Punjab, testing the Lodi sultans of Delhi.
steps.today: Today: Kabul, Afghanistan.

steps.title: The first battle of Panipat
steps.text: Babur meets Ibrahim Lodi, Sultan of Delhi, at Panipat. He ties carts together as a barrier, puts guns and matchlock men behind them and sends horse archers round the flanks. Babur puts his own army at 12,000 and Ibrahim’s at 100,000; both figures are doubted. Ibrahim dies on the field, and the Delhi Sultanate ends.
steps.today: Today: Panipat, Haryana, India.

steps.title: Khanwa
steps.text: Rana Sanga of Mewar, leader of a Rajput alliance, marches against Babur. Before the battle Babur swears off wine, pours it away, breaks his gold and silver cups and calls the war a holy war. At Khanwa, near Sikri, his guns and flank attacks win again. Rana Sanga escapes wounded and dies the next year.
steps.today: Today: Khanwa, Bharatpur district, Rajasthan, a few kilometres from Fatehpur Sikri.

steps.title: Gardens and a grave
steps.text: India is hot and dusty, Babur writes, without good horses, grapes or melons, but rich in gold and skilled workers. He lays out walled gardens with running water at Agra. He dies there in December 1530. His daughter Gulbadan later tells the family story that he gave his own life to save his sick son, Humayun.
steps.today: Today: the Ram Bagh, Agra. Babur was later buried in his garden at Kabul, the Bagh-e Babur.

steps.title: Defeated by Sher Khan
steps.text: Babur’s son Humayun struggles to hold the new empire against his brothers and the Afghans. Sher Khan, an Afghan chief from Bihar, surprises him at Chausa in 1539, and Humayun nearly drowns escaping across the Ganges. In 1540 Sher Khan beats him again near Kannauj, and Humayun flees west, ten years after his father’s death.
steps.today: Today: Kannauj, Uttar Pradesh; Chausa is in Buxar district, Bihar.

steps.title: Sher Shah’s roads and rupee
steps.text: Crowned as Sher Shah, the Afghan ruler reorganises the north in five years. He measures land for tax, rebuilds the great road from Bengal to the Indus, later called the Grand Trunk Road, with rest houses (sarais), and strikes a silver coin, the rupiya, ancestor of the rupee. He dies in 1545 in a gunpowder explosion at Kalinjar.
steps.today: Today: Sher Shah’s tomb stands in an artificial lake at Sasaram, Bihar.

steps.title: A birth in the desert
steps.text: Humayun wanders through Sindh and Rajasthan. At Umarkot, in October 1542, his young wife Hamida Banu Begum gives birth to a son, Akbar. Humayun then goes to Shah Tahmasp of Persia, who lends him troops in return for promises, Kandahar among them. In 1545 he takes Kandahar and Kabul from his own brothers.
steps.today: Today: Umarkot, Sindh, Pakistan.

steps.title: The fall on the library stairs
steps.text: Sher Shah’s empire splits after his son dies, and Humayun marches back. He wins at Sirhind in June 1555 and enters Delhi again in July. In January 1556, hurrying down the steep stairs of his library in Delhi’s old fort when he hears the call to prayer, he falls, and dies three days later.
steps.today: Today: the Sher Mandal, in the Purana Qila, Delhi.

steps.title: Hemu and the second Panipat
steps.text: Akbar, thirteen, is crowned in a garden at Kalanaur in the Punjab, with Bairam Khan as regent. Hemu, the Sur minister and general, takes Agra and Delhi and crowns himself Raja Vikramaditya. At Panipat an arrow strikes Hemu in the eye; his army breaks, and he is captured and beheaded. The Mughals are back to stay.
steps.today: Today: Panipat, Haryana; Kalanaur is in Gurdaspur district, Punjab.

steps.title: The Amber alliance
steps.text: Akbar takes power from Bairam Khan in 1560. In 1562 Raja Bharmal of Amber, a Kachhwaha Rajput, gives him his daughter in marriage; she will be the mother of Jahangir, and her family become great Mughal generals. Akbar also ends the enslaving of prisoners of war (1562) and the tax on non-Muslims (jizya, 1564).
steps.today: Today: Amer, near Jaipur, Rajasthan.

steps.title: The siege of Chittor
steps.text: Udai Singh of Mewar, Rana Sanga’s son, refuses to submit. Akbar besieges his great fort at Chittor for four months. Its commanders Jaimal and Patta die defending it, the fort’s women burn themselves (jauhar), and in February 1568 it falls. Akbar orders a massacre; a figure of 30,000 dead is often given and is disputed.
steps.today: Today: Chittorgarh, Rajasthan, a World Heritage site.

steps.title: The ride to Gujarat
steps.text: Akbar conquers Gujarat in 1572, winning its rich ports and a window on the sea, where he meets the Portuguese. When rebels rise in 1573 he rides from Fatehpur Sikri to Ahmedabad, some 800 kilometres, in eleven days with a small force, and defeats them. Gujarat stays Mughal for about 150 years.
steps.today: Today: Ahmedabad, Gujarat.

steps.title: Haldighati
steps.text: Udai Singh’s son, Maharana Pratap, will not submit either. Akbar sends an army under Raja Man Singh of Amber, and at the Haldighati pass Pratap’s smaller force is beaten after hard fighting. Pratap escapes, in tradition on his horse Chetak, who dies after carrying him to safety, and fights on from the hills.
steps.today: Today: Haldighati, Rajsamand district, Rajasthan.

steps.title: City of victory
steps.text: Akbar’s long-awaited son Salim is born in 1569 at Sikri, home of the Sufi saint Shaikh Salim Chishti. Akbar builds a new capital there in red sandstone, with palaces, a great mosque and the saint’s tomb, and after Gujarat names it Fatehpur, ‘city of victory’. The court leaves in 1585, and the city stands almost untouched.
steps.today: Today: Fatehpur Sikri, Agra district, Uttar Pradesh, a World Heritage site.

steps.title: The house of worship
steps.text: In a House of Worship (Ibadat Khana) Akbar hosts debates, first among Muslim scholars, then with Hindu, Jain and Zoroastrian teachers and Jesuit priests from Portuguese Goa. He comes to favour ‘peace with all’ (sulh-i kul). From 1582 he takes some courtiers as disciples, a circle later called the Divine Faith (Din-i Ilahi); historians debate whether it was a religion.
steps.today: Today: the site of the Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri is uncertain.

steps.title: Counting the empire
steps.text: Raja Todar Mal, Akbar’s finance minister, has land measured and taxed on ten years’ average yields. Every officer holds a rank (mansab) that sets his pay and the horsemen he must keep, and the empire is divided into provinces (subahs). Abul Fazl describes it all in the Ain-i Akbari. From 1585 to 1598 the court rules from Lahore.
steps.today: Today: Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan.

steps.title: Chand Bibi and the Deccan
steps.text: Akbar turns south. In 1595 Chand Bibi, regent of Ahmadnagar, defends its fort against his son Murad and wins a treaty. In 1600 she dies, killed by her own side or by her own hand (accounts differ), and the city falls. In 1601 Akbar takes the great fort of Asirgarh, near Burhanpur, after a long siege.
steps.today: Today: Ahilyanagar (Ahmednagar), Maharashtra; Asirgarh is in Burhanpur district, Madhya Pradesh.

steps.title: A son in revolt
steps.text: Prince Salim, impatient to rule, sets up his own court at Allahabad in 1600. In 1602 he has Abul Fazl, Akbar’s friend and historian, ambushed and killed by Bir Singh Deo Bundela. Father and son are reconciled in 1604. Akbar dies at Agra in October 1605, and Salim takes the throne as Jahangir, ‘world seizer’.
steps.today: Today: Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh; Akbar’s tomb is at Sikandra, Agra.

steps.title: The fifth Guru
steps.text: Guru Arjan, fifth Guru of the Sikhs, compiles the scripture later called the Guru Granth Sahib and installs it in the Harmandir Sahib at Amritsar in 1604. In 1606 Jahangir’s son Khusrau rebels and visits the Guru on his flight. Jahangir has the Guru arrested, and he dies in custody at Lahore, the first martyr of the Sikh faith.
steps.today: Today: Gurdwara Dera Sahib, Lahore, marks the place.

steps.title: An English ambassador
steps.text: Sir Thomas Roe, ambassador of James I of England, lands at Surat and reaches Jahangir’s court at Ajmer in 1616. He stays three years seeking trading rights and wins only limited favours. He describes an emperor who drinks heavily but hears petitions in public. Real power often lies with Jahangir’s wife, Nur Jahan, whose name appears on the coins.
steps.today: Today: Ajmer, Rajasthan, home of the shrine (dargah) of Muinuddin Chishti.

steps.title: Gardens of Kashmir
steps.text: Jahangir loves Kashmir. He lays out the Shalimar garden by the Dal lake, with terraces, channels and fountains. His painters, among them Mansur and Abu’l Hasan, paint birds, animals and flowers with a naturalist’s eye. In 1627 he dies on the way back from Kashmir, and is buried in a garden tomb at Lahore.
steps.today: Today: the Shalimar Bagh, Srinagar; Jahangir’s tomb is at Shahdara, Lahore.

steps.title: A tomb for Mumtaz
steps.text: Shah Jahan, emperor since 1628, loses his wife Mumtaz Mahal in 1631: she dies at Burhanpur giving birth to their fourteenth child. He builds her tomb in white marble inlaid with stones, beside the Yamuna at Agra: the Taj Mahal, finished about 1648, with the whole complex about 1653. Ustad Ahmad Lahori is usually named its architect.
steps.today: Today: the Taj Mahal, Agra, a World Heritage site.

steps.title: Shahjahanabad
steps.text: Shah Jahan builds a new capital at Delhi, Shahjahanabad, with a red sandstone fort on the Yamuna, the Red Fort, and the great Friday mosque, the Jama Masjid. His daughter Jahanara lays out the market street of Chandni Chowk. In the fort’s halls stands the jewelled Peacock Throne, which took seven years to make.
steps.today: Today: Old Delhi; the Red Fort is a World Heritage site.

steps.title: Brothers at war
steps.text: When Shah Jahan falls ill in 1657, his four sons fight for the throne. Dara Shikoh, the eldest, who had the Upanishads translated into Persian, is beaten by Aurangzeb and Murad at Samugarh, near Agra, in 1658. Aurangzeb confines his father in Agra fort, where he lives until 1666, and has Dara executed in Delhi in 1659.
steps.today: Today: Samugarh is a village near Agra; Shah Jahan’s rooms in Agra fort look out on the Taj.

steps.title: Shivaji
steps.text: In the hills of the western Deccan, Shivaji Bhonsle builds a Maratha state from forts taken from Bijapur. In 1659 Bijapur’s general Afzal Khan meets him for talks below Pratapgad, and Shivaji kills him; each side says the other struck first. In 1663 he raids the Mughal governor’s camp at Pune, and in 1664 he sacks Surat.
steps.today: Today: Pratapgad fort, Satara district, Maharashtra.

steps.title: Escape from Agra
steps.text: Besieged by Raja Jai Singh of Amber, Shivaji signs the treaty of Purandar in 1665 and gives up 23 forts. In 1666 he visits Aurangzeb at Agra, is slighted at court and kept under guard. He escapes, the popular story says hidden in baskets of sweets sent out as gifts, and is back in the Deccan within months.
steps.today: Today: Agra, Uttar Pradesh.

steps.title: Crowned at Raigad
steps.text: Shivaji wins back his forts and in 1674 is crowned king (Chhatrapati) at Raigad, with Vedic rites led by Gaga Bhatt of Varanasi. He has a council of eight ministers and a navy on the Konkan coast, and in 1677, allied with Golconda, campaigns far south to Jinji. He dies in 1680; his son Sambhaji takes up the war.
steps.today: Today: Raigad fort, Raigad district, Maharashtra.

steps.title: A stricter rule
steps.text: Aurangzeb, who takes the title Alamgir, ‘world conqueror’, rules as a strict Sunni. He orders major temples destroyed, among them the Vishwanath at Varanasi (1669) and the Keshava Deva at Mathura (1670), while granting land to others, and in 1679 restores the jizya. In 1675 the ninth Sikh Guru, Tegh Bahadur, is executed in Delhi.
steps.today: Today: Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Chandni Chowk, Delhi, marks the place of Guru Tegh Bahadur’s execution.

steps.title: The Khalsa
steps.text: Tegh Bahadur’s son, Guru Gobind Singh, makes Anandpur in the Shivalik hills his base. At the spring festival of Vaisakhi in 1699, Sikh tradition says, he calls for volunteers ready to give their heads, and initiates five as the first of the Khalsa, the initiated. He fights hill rajas and Mughal armies, and loses all four sons.
steps.today: Today: Anandpur Sahib, Rupnagar district, Punjab, India.

steps.title: The fall of Golconda
steps.text: In 1681 Aurangzeb leaves the north for good to fight in the Deccan. He takes Bijapur in 1686 and, in 1687, after an eight-month siege, Golconda, when a gate is opened to his army, it is said, by bribery. In 1689 Shivaji’s son Sambhaji is captured and executed. The empire is now at its widest.
steps.today: Today: Golconda fort, Hyderabad, Telangana; Bijapur is Vijayapura, Karnataka.

steps.title: A plain grave
steps.text: The Marathas fight on under Rajaram and then his widow Tarabai, and the war drags on for almost twenty years. Aurangzeb dies at Ahmadnagar in March 1707, aged 88. At his wish he is buried in an open grave at Khuldabad, near the shrine of a Sufi saint, paid for, it is said, with caps he sewed himself.
steps.today: Today: Khuldabad, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (Aurangabad) district, Maharashtra.

steps.title: The successor states
steps.text: After Aurangzeb, emperors come and go quickly, some made and unmade by nobles. Governors become rulers in all but name: Murshid Quli Khan in Bengal, the Nizam at Hyderabad, Saadat Khan in Awadh, while the Marathas push north. In 1717 the emperor Farrukhsiyar grants the English East India Company duty-free trade in Bengal.
steps.today: Today: Murshidabad, West Bengal, capital of the nawabs of Bengal from 1717.

steps.title: Nadir Shah
steps.text: Nadir Shah, the new ruler of Persia, invades and routs the Mughal army at Karnal in February 1739. In Delhi a riot kills some of his soldiers, and he orders a massacre; estimates of the dead, often 20,000 to 30,000, are disputed. He leaves with the treasury, the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond.
steps.today: Today: Karnal, Haryana; the Koh-i-Noor is in the British Crown Jewels.

steps.title: The third battle of Panipat
steps.text: After Plassey in 1757 the East India Company controls Bengal. In the north the Marathas, now the emperor’s protectors, face Ahmad Shah Durrani of Afghanistan at Panipat. In one of the century’s largest battles the Marathas are crushed; the dead are often put at more than 60,000, a disputed figure. The emperor, Shah Alam II, is far away.
steps.today: Today: the Kala Amb memorial, Panipat, marks the battlefield.

steps.title: From Delhi to Palam
steps.text: Shah Alam II joins the nawabs of Bengal and Awadh against the Company and loses at Buxar in 1764. At Allahabad in 1765 he grants it the right to collect Bengal’s revenue (diwani). He returns to Delhi in 1772 under Maratha protection, is blinded by the Rohilla Ghulam Qadir in 1788, and from 1803 lives under British protection.
steps.today: Today: a saying of the time ran ‘the realm of Shah Alam is from Delhi to Palam’, a village near the city.

steps.title: The last emperor
steps.text: In May 1857 rebel sepoys reach Delhi and proclaim the old emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, a poet in Urdu, their leader. British forces retake the city in September, and a British officer shoots two of his sons and a grandson. He is tried, deposed and exiled to Rangoon, where he dies in 1862. The Mughal dynasty is over.
steps.today: Today: his shrine (dargah) is in Yangon, Myanmar.

steps.title: The Mughal inheritance
steps.text: The Mughals leave a lasting mark. The Taj Mahal, Agra fort, Fatehpur Sikri, Humayun’s tomb and the Red Fort are World Heritage sites, the first two listed in 1983. Their courts helped shape Urdu, north Indian miniature painting, Hindustani music and much of the region’s cooking, and India’s prime minister speaks from the Red Fort each Independence Day.
steps.today: Today: Agra, Uttar Pradesh, and the Mughal monuments across India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Afghanistan.

items.name: Babur
items.text: A Timurid prince who lost his homeland, Babur won an empire in India at 43. He was a bold general, a poet in Turki and Persian and a keen gardener. His memoir, the Baburnama, is one of the earliest autobiographies in Islamic literature, frank about his defeats, his drinking and his doubts.

items.name: Gulbadan Begum
items.text: Babur’s daughter Gulbadan (‘rose body’) wrote the Humayun-nama at Akbar’s request, one of the few histories by a woman of her time. It describes family life, Humayun’s wanderings and his marriage to Hamida. In 1576 she led a party of royal women on the pilgrimage to Mecca, and was away about seven years.

items.name: Humayun
items.text: Babur’s eldest son lost the empire to Sher Shah and spent fifteen years in exile, part of it in Persia, before winning it back in 1555. He loved astronomy and books, and brought Persian painters to India who founded the Mughal painting workshop. His tomb in Delhi, built for him by his widow, foreshadows the Taj Mahal.

items.name: Sher Shah Suri
items.role: Afghan ruler of the Sur Empire
items.text: Born Farid, he took the name Sher Khan, it is said, after killing a tiger. From a small estate in Bihar he rose to drive Humayun out of India. In five years as emperor he reformed land revenue, coinage and roads, and much of his system was kept and extended by Akbar.

items.name: Bairam Khan
items.text: A Turkman noble and poet, Bairam Khan followed Humayun into exile and led his return. As regent for the young Akbar he won the second battle of Panipat. In 1560 Akbar took power himself and sent him on pilgrimage to Mecca; on the way, at Patan in Gujarat, he was killed by an Afghan with a grudge.

items.name: Hemu
items.text: From a merchant family of Rewari, Hemu rose to be chief minister and general of the Sur ruler Adil Shah, winning, the chronicles say, twenty-two battles. In 1556 he took Delhi and crowned himself Raja Vikramaditya. Wounded in the eye at Panipat, he was captured and beheaded.

items.name: Akbar
items.text: Crowned at thirteen, Akbar turned his grandfather’s conquest into a lasting empire through alliances with Rajput kings, a new tax system and a ranked nobility. He never learned to read, yet had books read to him daily and built a great library. Among the faiths he sought ‘peace with all’.

items.name: Abul Fazl
items.text: Abul Fazl wrote the Akbarnama, the official history of the reign, and the Ain-i Akbari, a survey of the empire’s provinces, revenues, customs and court. He championed Akbar’s ‘peace with all’. Prince Salim saw him as a rival, and on Salim’s orders he was ambushed and killed in 1602 on his way back from the Deccan.

items.name: Raja Todar Mal
items.text: Todar Mal served Sher Shah, then rose under Akbar as a general and finance minister. His land revenue system measured each field and set the tax on average yields and prices over ten years, and shaped revenue records long after. He is often counted among Akbar’s ‘nine jewels’, a later tradition.

items.name: Raja Man Singh
items.role: Raja of Amber and Mughal general
items.text: Adopted son of Raja Bhagwant Das of Amber, Man Singh became one of Akbar’s greatest generals. He led the Mughal army at Haldighati, governed Kabul, Bihar and Bengal, and built the Govind Dev temple at Vrindavan and much of Amber fort. He held one of the highest ranks in the empire, 7,000.

items.name: Maharana Pratap
items.text: Son of Udai Singh, Pratap refused to accept Mughal overlordship when other Rajput rulers did. After Haldighati he fought on from the Aravalli hills, and by his death had won back most of Mewar, though not Chittor. He is remembered across Rajasthan, and India, as a symbol of resistance.

items.name: Chand Bibi
items.text: Daughter of Hussain Nizam Shah I of Ahmadnagar and widow of Ali Adil Shah I of Bijapur, Chand Bibi acted as regent in both kingdoms. In 1595 she led the defence of Ahmadnagar, repairing a breach in the walls, it is said, overnight. She died in 1600 amid quarrels among the defenders, and the fort soon fell.

items.name: Jahangir
items.text: Born Salim at Sikri, Jahangir rebelled against his father but ruled for 22 years largely on his father’s lines. A keen naturalist, he had his painters record birds, animals and plants, and wrote a frank memoir, the Jahangirnama. He admits to his love of wine and opium, and left much business to Nur Jahan.

items.name: Nur Jahan
items.text: Born Mihr-un-Nissa, daughter of a Persian noble, she married Jahangir in 1611. As Nur Jahan, ‘light of the world’, she issued orders and coins in her own name, hunted tigers and brought her family to high office. She built her father’s marble tomb at Agra, the Itimad-ud-Daula, often called a forerunner of the Taj.

items.name: Guru Arjan
items.text: Guru Arjan completed the Harmandir Sahib at Amritsar, later called the Golden Temple, and compiled the Adi Granth from the hymns of the earlier Gurus, his own, and saints such as Kabir and Farid. His death in Mughal custody at Lahore made him the first Sikh martyr.

items.name: Shah Jahan
items.text: Born Khurram, he rebelled against his father before taking the throne in 1628. His reign was the empire’s richest, and he spent lavishly on building: the Taj Mahal, the Red Fort and the Jama Masjid at Delhi. Deposed by his son Aurangzeb in 1658, he spent his last eight years confined in Agra fort.

items.name: Mumtaz Mahal
items.text: Born Arjumand Banu Begum, a niece of Nur Jahan, she married Prince Khurram in 1612 and went with him even on campaign. They had fourteen children. She died at Burhanpur after the birth of the last, and her body was later carried to Agra, to the tomb now called the Taj Mahal.

items.name: Jahanara Begum
items.text: After her mother’s death Jahanara ran the imperial household as first lady (Padshah Begum) and grew rich, partly from trade through Surat. She laid out Chandni Chowk, wrote lives of Sufi saints, and shared her father’s captivity in Agra fort until his death. She lies in a simple grave at Nizamuddin, Delhi.

items.name: Dara Shikoh
items.text: Shah Jahan’s favourite son, Dara studied Sufism and Hindu philosophy. He had fifty Upanishads translated into Persian and wrote The Meeting of the Two Oceans, on what Islam and Hinduism share. Beaten by Aurangzeb, he was paraded through Delhi and executed in 1659, condemned as an apostate.

items.name: Aurangzeb
items.text: Aurangzeb seized the throne in 1658 and ruled for 49 years, taking the empire to its widest. A devout, austere Sunni, he ruled by Islamic law and copied the Quran by hand. Historians still argue over his record on temples and the jizya, and over his long Deccan wars, which many see as draining the empire.

items.name: Shivaji
items.text: Son of Shahji Bhonsle, a general of Bijapur, and Jijabai, Shivaji built a kingdom from hill forts and swift light cavalry, fighting both Bijapur and the Mughals. Crowned Chhatrapati in 1674, he used Marathi in government and built sea forts such as Sindhudurg. Maharashtra remembers him as its founding hero.

items.name: Guru Gobind Singh
items.text: The tenth Sikh Guru was nine when his father, Guru Tegh Bahadur, was executed. He founded the Khalsa in 1699 and fought the hill rajas and Mughal armies, losing all four sons. He named the scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, as Guru after him, and died at Nanded in the Deccan in 1708.

items.name: Tarabai
items.text: Widow of Shivaji’s son Rajaram, Tarabai ruled for her young son from 1700 and led the war against Aurangzeb, sending raids deep into Mughal lands. After his death she lost a struggle for power to Sambhaji’s son Shahu, but stayed a force in Maratha politics into old age.

items.name: Bahadur Shah Zafar
items.text: Emperor in name only, living on a Company pension, Bahadur Shah II wrote poetry in Urdu under the pen name Zafar, ‘victory’, and was a patron of Ghalib. Proclaimed leader of the 1857 uprising, he was tried by the British and exiled to Rangoon, where he died. His grave there was found again in 1991.
